summary: Defines the syntax used by the World-Wide Web to encode names and addresses of objects on the network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A URI gives a common form for naming or locating an object on a network. Its scheme identifies how to interpret the rest of the identifier.

questions: what is the difference between a uri and a url
subtitle: A common syntax for naming and addressing objects through different network schemes.

tldr.problem: The Web needed a common way to represent names and addresses from many different protocols and naming systems.
tldr.mechanism: A URI begins with a scheme and colon followed by a scheme-specific path. Percent escapes represent characters that cannot be used directly, and partial forms can refer to a resource in context.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1630 records existing Web practice and is Informational. Its IESG note says a general Resource Identifier standard was under development when the memo was published.

today: RFC 1630 is an Informational memo and does not specify an Internet standard. Its IESG note said a standard for general Resource Identifiers was under development when the memo was published.

sections.title: URIs, URLs, and URNs
sections.content:
RFC 1630 describes the syntax used by the World-Wide Web to encode names and addresses of network objects. A Universal Resource Identifier (URI) belongs to a registered name space or refers to a registered protocol or name space.

A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is a kind of URI that expresses an address and access method. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) was being discussed as a more persistent name; this memo does not define URNs. The document records existing practice and says the syntax had been used by Web software since 1990.
sections.plainLanguage: A URI names an object or gives its network address. A URL is a URI that describes how to access an object; this memo does not define URNs.

sections.title: Why Use One URI Syntax
sections.content:
Different network protocols and data formats can be connected or converted, but names and addresses are often passed between people and documents and may last a long time. The memo therefore describes a way to label a name with the name space it belongs to.

The design aims to be extensible, complete, and printable. A registered scheme name comes first and identifies how to interpret the rest. Escaping allows otherwise unsafe characters to be represented using a limited character set.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared syntax lets a document refer to objects from different systems. The scheme label tells software which naming rules to use.

sections.title: URI Parts and Reserved Characters
sections.content:
A complete URI consists of a scheme, a colon, and a path whose format depends on the scheme. When a path contains slashes, they indicate a hierarchy. The memo reserves punctuation for particular uses: slash for path divisions, hash for a fragment, and question mark for a query.

A fragment identifier follows a hash and names a part or sub-function within an object; its meaning comes from the application or content type. The memo cautions that a URI is not a file name, even when its path resembles a directory structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme and colon come first, followed by a path interpreted using that scheme's rules. Special characters mark boundaries such as path parts, queries, and fragments.

sections.title: Percent Escapes
sections.content:
In the memo's conventional encoding, a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits represents a character that cannot safely appear directly. A percent sign always introduces an escape. Before comparing two URIs, systems may need to bring them to the same encoding level.

Reserved characters must not be freely changed between escaped and unescaped forms because their meaning changes. For example, an encoded hyphen can be equivalent to a literal hyphen, but an encoded slash does not act as a path separator.
sections.plainLanguage: A percent sign and two hexadecimal digits stand for a character that cannot safely appear in a URI. Reserved punctuation keeps its meaning, so encoding it can change the URI.

sections.title: Relative URI Forms
sections.content:
Within an object whose URI is known, a reference can omit parts shared with that context. This lets related objects refer to each other with shorter forms and can allow a group of objects to move without changing every reference.

The memo defines how to expand a partial form using the context URI, including rules for schemes, slashes, and dot path segments. Outside a well-controlled context, it says to use the full form.
sections.plainLanguage: A relative URI leaves out parts that match the address of the current object. Software combines it with that context to form the full URI.

sections.title: Schemes and Registration
sections.content:
The memo describes schemes including http, ftp, gopher, mailto, news, telnet, wais, and file. It reserves urn: for work on Uniform Resource Names and proposes that new schemes be registered through IANA.

A new scheme must define how to retrieve objects it names. Experimental scheme prefixes must begin with x-. The memo's Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme label identifies the naming system, and new schemes can be added. The memo proposes a registration process and requires each scheme to define how its objects are retrieved.
